why_this_tool: OpenAI Evals puts datasets, code and model graders, human annotation, eval runs and trace grading for agents in one place, so every layer of this lesson can be practised against the same test set.
alternatives: promptfoo (local, config-file driven, runs from the command line with no hosted account), Inspect AI (Python framework with strong agent and sandbox support), LangSmith and Braintrust (hosted tracing plus datasets and experiment comparison), the Anthropic Console evaluation tool (prompt-centric test cases in a web console), and pytest (plain code assertions with no built-in model graders or run history).

setup.do: Install the OpenAI CLI on your laptop using the package installer named in the installation section.
setup.done_when: Asking the CLI for its version or help text prints a result in your terminal.
setup.why: The CLI lets you drive requests and collect outputs from a terminal, which you will reuse when you automate eval runs at the end of the path.

setup.do: Create a dedicated project, a service account and an API key for your eval practice; note that this is a hosted API with usage billing, so keep the test set small.
setup.done_when: A new project exists with a service account and you hold one API key scoped to it.

verified.section_found: Create a project, service account, and API key

setup.why: A separate project keeps eval runs, datasets and spend apart from other work, and a service account key is what an automated job would use later.

setup.do: Configure CLI authentication with the new key through an environment variable, not a file in your repository.
setup.done_when: The CLI reports that it is authenticated without you pasting the key into a command.
setup.why: Every later step calls the API, and keeping the key in the environment is the habit that carries over to CI.

setup.do: Send one first request from the CLI to confirm the whole stack works end to end.
setup.done_when: A model response to your test prompt is printed in the terminal.
setup.why: A single successful call rules out key, project and network problems before you start building evals on top.

steps.do: Create a dataset by uploading a CSV of 15 to 20 realistic inputs with expected outputs for one task you know well, such as ticket classification.
steps.done_when: The dataset shows your rows with an input column and an expected output column.

source.title: Getting started with datasets | OpenAI API

steps.why: A test set drawn from real cases is the foundation of every later measurement. Starting small keeps cost low and makes you read every row.

steps.do: Write the success criteria for the task as three to five checkable statements, using the testing and verification guidance to decide what the model must prove about its own output.
steps.done_when: You have a short written list where each criterion can be answered pass or fail for a single output.
steps.why: Criteria written before any grader exists stop you from tuning the eval to whatever the model already does. Each statement becomes one grader later.

steps.do: Create an eval for the task by defining the data source schema and one code-style testing criterion that compares the output with the expected label.
steps.done_when: The API returns an eval identifier and the eval lists your schema and one testing criterion.

verified.section_found: Create an eval for a task

steps.why: The eval object, its item schema and its testing criteria are the core model of the tool. A deterministic check is the fastest and cheapest grader layer.

steps.do: Load your test set into the platform as a JSONL file whose fields match the eval schema.
steps.done_when: The upload returns a file identifier and the row count matches your local file.
steps.why: Persisting test data as a versioned file means every run is graded against exactly the same items, which is what makes runs comparable.

steps.do: Create an eval run that applies your prompt to the uploaded test data and grades each output.
steps.done_when: The run reaches a completed status and reports pass and fail counts.
steps.why: A run ties one prompt and one model to one score, turning a vague sense of quality into a stored number.

steps.do: Add a model grader to the dataset that scores one criterion a string check cannot judge, such as whether the explanation is faithful to the input.
steps.done_when: Each row shows a grader score next to the generated output.

source.title: Getting started with datasets | OpenAI API

steps.why: Model-graded checks cover quality dimensions that code assertions miss. You need to see where they agree and disagree with your own judgment.

steps.do: Annotate every generated output yourself with a pass or fail rating and a short note, then compare your ratings with the model grader's scores.
steps.done_when: You can name the rows where your rating and the grader's score disagree and say why.

source.title: Getting started with datasets | OpenAI API

steps.why: Human labels are the reference that tells you whether a model grader can be trusted. The notes are the raw material for error analysis.

steps.do: Compare two eval runs of the same eval, one per prompt variant, and group the failing rows into named failure categories.
steps.done_when: You have a short table of failure categories with a count per run and a decision on which prompt to keep.
steps.why: Error analysis on failures tells you what to change next. Comparing runs shows whether the change fixed that category without breaking another.

steps.do: Configure every run with an explicitly named model version instead of a default, and record it beside the prompt version.
steps.done_when: Rerunning the eval with the same pinned model and prompt gives a score close to the first run.
steps.why: A score only means something when you know exactly which model produced it. Pinning the model is the first requirement for a reproducible eval.

steps.do: Run trace grading on a small agent that calls at least one function tool, with a grader that checks the tool calls and their order as well as the final answer.
steps.done_when: At least one trace is marked as failed because of a step inside the trajectory, not because of the final message.
steps.why: For agents the unit under test is the whole trajectory. A correct final message can hide a wrong tool call or a skipped step.

steps.do: Create a dataset from the agent cases you just debugged and run it as a repeatable eval run.
steps.done_when: The agent cases run as an eval run with a score you can compare across agent versions.

verified.section_found: Move to datasets and eval runs when you need repeatability

steps.why: Traces are for understanding behavior, while datasets and runs are for proving that it stays fixed. This move is how a one-off finding becomes a regression test.

steps.do: Write a small script that starts the eval run, retries transient failures, and exits with an error when the pass rate drops below your threshold; run it the way a CI job would, using only the service account key.
steps.done_when: The script exits cleanly on your good prompt and fails on a deliberately worsened prompt.
steps.why: An eval in the delivery loop must run unattended and must separate a flaky API call from a real quality regression. This is the closest laptop equivalent of a gated pipeline.
